yes_case.case: The closest historical episodes are the August 2023 iCRR implementation and the demonetization liquidity absorption of November 2016. In August 2023, the RBI deployed a temporary 10% iCRR on incremental NDTL to mop up systemic liquidity surges driven by the return of Rs 2,000 banknotes and government spending. Unlike that past episode—which was unwound smoothly ahead of the festive season—the current dynamic differs because the liquidity overhang stems from structural foreign portfolio inflows and persistent forex interventions by the RBI that require permanent or semi-permanent sterilization rather than a short-term liquidity buffer. Furthermore, compared to the 2016 demonetization shock which was a one-off structural anomaly, the current environment features sustained macroeconomic volatility in domestic credit-deposit growth mismatches, making the iCRR a preferred targeted instrument to drain localized banking sector excess liquidity without altering the broader policy rate stance.
key_evidence: RBI August 2023 implementation of a 10% incremental cash reserve ratio (iCRR) on NDTL between May 19 and July 28, 2023.
November 2016 incremental CRR announcement requiring 100% CRR on incremental deposits following demonetization.
yes_case.strength_reason: The historical precedent of August 2023 proves the RBI views iCRR as an active, viable tool in its current operational toolkit for liquidity management, though differences in the underlying drivers of excess liquidity alter the exact mechanics of deployment.
yes_case.deliberately_ignored: RBI monetary policy committee meeting dates, liquidity deficit/surplus quantum calculations, statutory reserve requirement percentages, and broadcast schedules of RBI governor statements.

no_case.case: The closest past episode of liquidity management via the Reserve Bank of India was the August 2023 imposition of an incremental cash reserve ratio (iCRR) following the withdrawal of 2000-rupee notes, and the earlier 2016 demonetization liquidity absorption. The current setup differs fundamentally because those prior episodes were reactive measures designed to instantly mop up massive, discrete surges of sudden liquidity injections into the banking system caused by specific currency policy shocks. By contrast, the present macroeconomic environment features persistent, structural credit-deposit growth imbalances rather than a sudden, one-off surge of high-powered money, making broad-brush iCRR tools an excessively blunt and inappropriate instrument compared to standard variable rate reverse repo operations. Because the structural liquidity deficits or surpluses currently managed by the RBI do not match the discrete, massive currency-return shocks of August 2023 or November 2016, the historical precedent for deploying an iCRR does not fit the current transmission mechanism.

The Governor and the Monetary Policy Committee possess the direct executive will to deploy liquidity management tools rapidly when confronted with inflationary pressures or sudden surges in bank deposits. Because the principals at the RBI want to maintain macroeconomic stability and possess the unilateral, unhindered operational capability to issue and enforce an iCRR directive directly to commercial banks, they can deliver this policy decision instantaneously through their own internal administrative mechanisms.
